summary:
The Falkland Islands are a British Overseas Territory with their own Legislative Assembly, which legislates locally. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989 and the age of consent has been equal since 2005.

Same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017. The Legislative Assembly passed the bill in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general confirmed by reply in June 2017 that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples. A public consultation ahead of the bill recorded 90% support for same-sex marriage and 94% for civil partnerships in a territory of roughly 3,000 residents.

The Constitution Order 2008, at Article 16, bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The provision covers sexual orientation only; no gender-identity ground is identified in the constitutional text.

The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Falkland Islands. Defence is a United Kingdom responsibility; the islands legislate on domestic matters through their own assembly.

Legal gender change has been possible since 2014 under the Criminal Procedure and Evidence Ordinance 2014, which also recognises holders of United Kingdom gender recognition certificates as their acquired gender. There is no self-identification procedure and no non-binary legal category.

Hate-crime provisions are limited to sexual orientation. The Crimes Ordinance 2014 creates an offence of stirring up hatred on grounds of sexual orientation, and the Criminal Procedure and Evidence Ordinance 2014 makes sexual orientation an aggravating factor in sentencing. Neither instrument names gender identity or gender expression.

Stepchild and joint adoption by same-sex couples has been available since 2017. The Prisons Ordinance 2017 forms part of the custodial framework; the sources do not set out its provisions on the placement or treatment of transgender prisoners.

Attitudes in the territory are reported as largely positive, consistent with the consultation results.
tangentialFactors:
The Falkland Islands are a separate jurisdiction from South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, another British Overseas Territory. The registrar general confirmed in June 2017 that same-sex marriage is not legal in South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, so the marriage and civil partnership regime that applies in the Falklands does not carry across to that dependency.

The Falkland Islands sit outside the United Kingdom's domestic equality and gender recognition legislation. A visitor's legal position here is governed by local ordinances and the Constitution Order 2008, not by the protections that apply in the United Kingdom itself.
localsOnly:
Residents can marry or enter a civil partnership, and civil partnership is open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples. Adoption, including stepchild and joint adoption, has been open since 2017.

Changing legal gender requires the procedure under the Criminal Procedure and Evidence Ordinance 2014; there is no self-identification route and no non-binary category. United Kingdom gender recognition certificates are recognised as establishing acquired gender.

Hate-crime protection for residents covers sexual orientation only. Stirring up hatred on grounds of sexual orientation is an offence under the Crimes Ordinance 2014, and sexual orientation is a sentencing aggravating factor under the Criminal Procedure and Evidence Ordinance 2014. Gender identity is not named in either provision.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not record any prosecution or enforcement action under the sexual-orientation hate-crime provisions, so the practical reach of those offences is unresolved.

No information was identified on how the Prisons Ordinance 2017 handles the placement of transgender prisoners, or on custodial practice for transgender detainees.

No data was identified on trans-specific violence in the Falkland Islands. The sources also do not describe how a visitor would change a passport or identity marker, or whether local practice recognises a gender different from that recorded at birth for visitors.

Whether gender identity is covered by any non-discrimination provision outside the Constitution Order 2008 is not sourced.
